questions.stem: The stomach produces hydrochloric acid (pH 1-2). What are two functions of this acid?

options.text: To dissolve food and kill bacteria
To provide the optimum pH for pepsin and to kill harmful microorganisms in food
To neutralise bile and break down fats
To absorb nutrients and destroy vitamins

questions.explanation: Stomach acid creates the acidic environment (pH 1-2) needed for the protease enzyme pepsin to work at its optimum. It also kills most bacteria and pathogens that enter the body with food, providing a defence against infection. The acid does not absorb nutrients -- that happens in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Food moves through the digestive system by peristalsis. What is peristalsis?

options.text: Chemical breakdown of food by enzymes
Rhythmic contractions of smooth muscle in the gut wall that push food along
The absorption of nutrients through villi
The mixing of food with saliva in the mouth

questions.explanation: Peristalsis involves waves of circular muscle contraction behind the food bolus and relaxation ahead of it, squeezing food along the digestive tract. This is an involuntary process controlled by the autonomic nervous system. It occurs throughout the oesophagus, stomach, and intestines.

questions.stem: A patient has their gallbladder removed. Which aspect of digestion would be most affected?

options.text: Protein digestion in the stomach
Fat digestion in the small intestine, because bile (stored in the gallbladder) helps emulsify fats
Starch digestion in the mouth
Water absorption in the large intestine

questions.explanation: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, which is produced by the liver. Bile emulsifies fats (breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones), increasing the surface area for lipase enzymes to work on. Without the gallbladder, bile still reaches the intestine directly from the liver but is less concentrated, making fat digestion less efficient.

questions.stem: The small intestine is approximately 6-7 metres long in humans. Why is this length important for digestion and absorption?

options.text: It allows food to be stored for longer periods
It provides a large surface area and sufficient time for complete digestion and absorption of nutrients
It gives bacteria time to ferment the food
It allows all water to be removed from the food

questions.explanation: The length of the small intestine ensures that food has sufficient contact time with digestive enzymes for complete digestion, and passes over a large surface area of villi for maximum nutrient absorption. If the intestine were shorter, nutrients would pass through too quickly and be lost in the faeces.

questions.stem: The large intestine's main function is absorbing water from undigested food material. What would happen if the large intestine could not absorb water properly?

options.text: The person would become obese
The person would experience diarrhoea and could become dehydrated
Protein digestion would stop
The stomach would produce more acid

questions.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water from the remaining food material, forming solid faeces. If this process fails (as in infections like cholera), water remains in the gut, causing watery diarrhoea. This rapid water loss can lead to severe dehydration, which can be life-threatening if not treated with oral rehydration therapy.
